answer: Kafka's parallelism is limited by its number of partitions; for a fan-out to millions (e.g. Justin Bieber's 10-15 million followers) Kafka alone is painfully slow with a limited number of partitions, and adding a large number of partitions becomes a problem of its own. Fix: club a message stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with a message broker (SQS or RabbitMQ) to get a very high degree of fan-out; per-user delivery work goes to a queue many workers can drain (AWS: SNS topic pushing to subscribed SQS queues). One broker that broadcasts is not what happens at scale.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3 'How notification systems fan out': 'Kafka's parallelism is limited by its number of partitions... Kafka alone is painfully slow when you have a limited number of partitions... club a message stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with a message broker (SQS or RabbitMQ)'

answer: On a 2xx response it checks the header (first bytes) of the returned bytes, decides the format (e.g. 'this is a PNG'), invokes the matching decoder and renders the decoded image as pixels. evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'On a 2xx response the browser checks the header of the bytes it got back, decides the format... invokes the matching decoder and renders the decoded image as pixels'

Query the source of truth vs keep things pre-computed.

Source of truth when you need strong consistency, or as a startup with modest traffic; pre-compute (or store in a directly consumable form) for efficiency, when millions are concurrently active, at the price of keeping it updated yourself with extra write flows.

Redis (as a simplification; any key-value store whose value can be a set works, e.g. MongoDB). Key is the user id, value a set of user ids; the key highlight is reusing the set the database gives you so you don't check-and-set yourself.
Get status API: talks to Redis, counts the elements of the user's set (SCARD) and returns the count for the badge. Clear API: on tapping the icon, deletes the user's key in Redis (DEL).

If the user is already on the messaging tab, an arriving message (even in another conversation) isn't newly unread and needs no badge update; with WebSockets the backend can check whether the client's socket is off (e.g. watching reels) and only then update Redis.

It knows when a message could not be delivered to the user: it's the source of truth for delivery (delivered?, which tab, WebSocket up?), since persistent connections end at its edge servers (or it asks an online/offline service).

An event the messaging service publishes, an umbrella for every case in which the badge should bump: any message that couldn't be delivered to the user in real time; the where-is-the-user if/else logic lives there.
Which user sent which message to whom: { src, dest, msg }. Consumers (status update workers) add the sender to the recipient's set in Redis, e.g. B: {C, D} (SADD B C).

Read path: app calls get_status / clean_status on a status check API, which reads (counts) or deletes the user's set in a Redis cluster. Write path: messaging service's ON_MSG_UNSENT events via Kafka, pulled by status update workers that add the sender to the recipient's set (SADD); the stream also feeds the notification system; a note says writes can be batched if partitioned by recipient. Final version: workers first check an auxiliary Redis and write to main only for new senders; a clear deletes in both.
